entry.title: Solving Exercism’s Secret Handshake in Java

link.title: Solving Exercism’s Secret Handshake in Java

entry.content:
Introduction

Exercism is a free, open-source platform that offers hundreds of coding exercises across dozens of programming languages. Each exercise is designed to push you toward idiomatic, clean code — not just a solution that passes the tests, but one that demonstrates an understanding of the language and its standard library. The Java track is particularly rich because it forces you to think about types, generics, and the JVM ecosystem from the very first exercise.

This post walks through the Secret Handshake exercise end-to-end: what the problem is, how the project is structured, how Gradle orchestrates the build and the tests, how to open everything correctly in IntelliJ IDEA, and finally how to arrive at a clean solution using binary operations and Java collections. Before the solution, there is a dedicated section on the theory of binary numbers — unsigned, signed, and two’s complement — because understanding this foundation is what makes bitwise code feel natural rather than mysterious. The post closes with a rigorous analysis of time and space complexity.

What Is the Problem?

The Secret Handshake exercise asks you to write a function that takes an integer and returns a list of actions — a “secret handshake” — based on the binary representation of that number. The five least-significant bits of the input each encode a specific meaning:

Bit position Decimal value Binary mask Action
0 1 00001 wink
1 2 00010 double blink
2 4 00100 close your eyes
3 8 01000 jump
4 16 10000 reverse the order of the other actions

If bit 0 is set, you add wink to the list. If bit 1 is set, you add double blink, and so on. The first four bits build the list in a fixed order (wink → double blink → close your eyes → jump). The fifth bit is special: if it is set, you reverse the entire list before returning it.

A few examples to make this concrete:

  • 1 → binary 00001 → only bit 0 is set → [wink]
  • 3 → binary 00011 → bits 0 and 1 are set → [wink, double blink]
  • 19 → binary 10011 → bits 0, 1, and 4 are set → start with [wink, double blink], then reverse → [double blink, wink]
  • 26 → binary 11010 → bits 1, 3, and 4 are set → start with [double blink, jump], then reverse → [jump, double blink]

The elegance of this problem is that it maps perfectly onto bitwise AND operations — there is no need to parse strings, loop over digits, or use recursion. The processor already knows how to interrogate individual bits in constant time.

Project Structure

When you download the exercise from Exercism or browse the exercism/java repository on GitHub, the directory for this exercise looks like this:

secret-handshake/
├── build.gradle                          ← Gradle build script
├── gradlew                               ← Unix Gradle Wrapper script
├── gradlew.bat                           ← Windows Gradle Wrapper script
├── gradle/
│   └── wrapper/
│       ├── gradle-wrapper.jar            ← Wrapper bootstrap JAR
│       └── gradle-wrapper.properties     ← Wrapper configuration (Gradle version)
└── src/
    ├── main/
    │   └── java/
    │       └── SecretHandshake.java      ← your implementation
    └── test/
        └── java/
            └── SecretHandshakeTest.java  ← provided tests (do not modify)

Notice that there is no settings.gradle file. This is intentional: the exercise is a single, self-contained module. There are no sub-projects, no module dependencies, and no Kotlin build scripts. It is as minimal as a Gradle project can be while still being fully functional.

Your only job is to fill in the body of SecretHandshake.java. The test file is given to you and you should never modify it.

What Is Gradle and Why Does This Project Use It?

Gradle is an open-source build automation tool designed primarily for JVM-based projects. It handles three things that every non-trivial Java project needs: dependency management, compilation, and test execution.

Historically, Java projects used either Ant (which required you to write every step of the build by hand in XML) or Maven (which introduced a declarative, convention-based approach using a pom.xml file). Gradle combines the best of both worlds: it follows Maven’s conventions (so you rarely need to configure anything), but it uses a Groovy or Kotlin DSL instead of XML, making build scripts dramatically more readable and flexible.

For Exercism exercises, Gradle serves two practical purposes. First, it downloads and caches the test dependencies (JUnit 5 and AssertJ) automatically from Maven Central, so you never have to manually manage JAR files. Second, it provides the test task, which compiles your solution alongside the test file and runs all the test cases, reporting which ones pass and which ones fail.

The Gradle Wrapper

The gradlew script (and gradlew.bat on Windows) is called the Gradle Wrapper. Its purpose is to make the project self-contained with respect to the Gradle version: when you run ./gradlew test, the wrapper reads gradle/wrapper/gradle-wrapper.properties to find out which Gradle version the project expects, downloads it automatically if it is not already on your machine, and then delegates to it. This means you do not need Gradle installed globally — just a working JDK and the wrapper scripts are enough.

The build.gradle File

Here is the complete build script for this exercise:

plugins {
    id "java"
}

repositories {
    mavenCentral()
}

dependencies {
    testImplementation platform("org.junit:junit-bom:5.10.0")
    testImplementation "org.junit.jupiter:junit-jupiter"
    testImplementation "org.assertj:assertj-core:3.25.1"

    testRuntimeOnly "org.junit.platform:junit-platform-launcher"
}

test {
    useJUnitPlatform()

    testLogging {
        exceptionFormat = "full"
        showStandardStreams = true
        events = ["passed", "failed", "skipped"]
    }
}

Let us walk through it section by section.

plugins { id "java" } — This applies the Java plugin, which teaches Gradle how to compile .java files, how to find source files in src/main/java/ and test files in src/test/java/, and how to produce a compiled output. Without this plugin, Gradle would not know this is a Java project.

repositories { mavenCentral() } — This tells Gradle where to download dependencies from. Maven Central is the world’s largest public repository of JVM libraries, hosted at https://repo1.maven.org/maven2. When you declare a dependency, Gradle will look it up here by its group ID, artifact ID, and version number.

dependencies { ... } — This block declares which external libraries the project needs. Notice that all four entries use either testImplementation or testRuntimeOnly, never implementation. This means these libraries are only available during compilation and execution of tests — they are never bundled into any production artifact. The production code (your solution) has no external dependencies at all.

The four dependency entries are:

  • platform("org.junit:junit-bom:5.10.0") — A Bill of Materials (BOM). Instead of specifying the version of every JUnit 5 component individually, the BOM manages all versions as a consistent set. This prevents subtle incompatibility bugs between JUnit sub-modules.
  • org.junit.jupiter:junit-jupiter — The JUnit 5 API. This is what provides @Test, @DisplayName, @ParameterizedTest, and all the annotations you see in the test file.
  • org.assertj:assertj-core:3.25.1 — AssertJ is a fluent assertion library. Instead of writing assertEquals(expected, actual), AssertJ lets you write assertThat(actual).containsExactly("wink", "double blink"), which reads almost like English and produces much more informative error messages on failure.
  • org.junit.platform:junit-platform-launcher (runtime only) — The launcher is the bridge between Gradle and JUnit 5. It discovers and executes tests at runtime. It is declared as testRuntimeOnly because it is not needed at compile time.

test { useJUnitPlatform() } — This tells the Gradle test task to use the JUnit Platform as its test discovery engine. Without this line, Gradle would default to the older JUnit 4 runner and would not be able to find or execute JUnit 5 tests.

Opening the Project Correctly in IntelliJ IDEA

This is the step that causes the most confusion, and it is worth dwelling on. The golden rule is: always open the exercise folder itself — never a parent folder.

If you open a parent directory (for example, the entire exercism/java repository root), IntelliJ will detect the top-level settings.gradle that aggregates all exercises as Gradle sub-projects. IntelliJ then tries to run a Kotlin build script analysis task on every sub-project, including secret-handshake, which does not use Kotlin DSL. This produces the following misleading error:

Task 'prepareKotlinBuildScriptModel' not found in 
project ':practice:secret-handshake'.
BUILD FAILED

The fix is straightforward:

  1. File → Close Project (if another project is already open)
  2. File → Open → navigate to secret-handshake/ and open that specific directory
  3. IntelliJ detects build.gradle and shows a popup: “Trust and open Gradle project?” → click Trust
  4. The IDE syncs the project, and Gradle downloads JUnit 5 and AssertJ in the background
  5. After syncing, the Gradle tool window (View → Tool Windows → Gradle) shows the task tree with verification → test available

If you have already cloned the full repository and prefer not to copy the folder, you can create a minimal settings.gradle directly inside secret-handshake/:

rootProject.name = 'secret-handshake'

Then, in the Gradle tool window, click the + icon (Link Gradle project) and point it to the build.gradle file inside secret-handshake/. IntelliJ will treat it as the root of a new, independent Gradle project and will not inherit the parent module structure.

How to Approach This Type of Exercise

Before writing a single line of code, the most productive habit is to read the test file carefully. The test file is the specification. It tells you exactly what method signature you need to implement, what types are involved, what the expected output is for every meaningful input, and what edge cases the exercise author considered important.

For this exercise, the test file reveals:

  • The class name must be SecretHandshake (not Solution, not Main)
  • The method signature is something like List<String> calculateHandshake(int number) (or using a Signal enum if the test file imports one)
  • The tests cover a variety of inputs, including 0 (empty list), single-bit numbers, multi-bit numbers, and numbers where bit 16 triggers a reversal

Once you understand the interface, the next step is to think about the simplest possible representation of the problem. Here, the problem is inherently binary. The input is a number; each bit is a yes/no flag. The output is a list of strings whose contents and order depend on which flags are active. There is no recursion, no graph traversal, no dynamic programming. The challenge is purely about reading bits correctly and building a list in the right order.

Binary Numbers: Theory You Actually Need

Before diving into the Java-specific implementation, it is worth building a solid mental model of how binary numbers work — both in the unsigned (non-negative only) sense and in the signed two’s complement representation that Java uses for all integer types. This section is self-contained: if you already know this material, skip ahead; if not, everything in the implementation section will make much more sense after reading it.

The Positional Value System

The decimal system we use every day is a base-10 positional system: each digit position represents a power of 10. Reading from right to left, the positions represent 10⁰ = 1, 10¹ = 10, 10² = 100, and so on.

Binary is a base-2 positional system: each digit (called a bit) represents a power of 2. Reading from right to left, the positions represent 2⁰ = 1, 2¹ = 2, 2² = 4, 2³ = 8, 2⁴ = 16, and so on. A bit can only be 0 or 1.

Converting from binary to decimal is a matter of summing the positional values for every bit that is 1. For example:

Binary:  1  0  1  1  0
         │  │  │  │  └── 2⁰ = 1  × 0 =  0
         │  │  │  └───── 2¹ = 2  × 1 =  2
         │  │  └──────── 2² = 4  × 1 =  4
         │  └─────────── 2³ = 8  × 0 =  0
         └────────────── 2⁴ = 16 × 1 = 16
                                      ────
                                      22

So 10110 in binary equals 22 in decimal.

How Many Values Can N Bits Represent?

This is one of the most useful formulas to internalize. With N bits, where each bit can be either 0 or 1, and all combinations are independent, the total number of distinct patterns is:

2^N

This follows directly from the multiplication principle of combinatorics: two choices for the first bit, two for the second, two for the third, and so on — multiplied together gives 2 × 2 × … × 2 = 2^N.

N bits Distinct patterns (2^N) Unsigned range
1 2 0 to 1
2 4 0 to 3
3 8 0 to 7
4 16 0 to 15
5 32 0 to 31
8 256 0 to 255
16 65 536 0 to 65 535
32 4 294 967 296 0 to 4 294 967 295

For the Secret Handshake exercise, only 5 bits matter. Those 5 bits produce 2⁵ = 32 distinct patterns, ranging from 00000 (= 0, no actions) to 11111 (= 31, all four actions reversed). Any bits beyond position 4 are irrelevant and should be masked away before processing.

Unsigned vs. Signed Integers

An unsigned integer uses all N bits to represent magnitude. With N bits, unsigned integers cover the range from 0 to 2^N − 1.

A signed integer needs to represent negative values as well. The simplest scheme, sign-magnitude, uses the most significant bit (MSB) as a sign flag (0 = positive, 1 = negative) and the remaining N−1 bits for magnitude. However, sign-magnitude has two representations of zero (+0 and −0), which complicates arithmetic in hardware.

Modern computers — and Java — use two’s complement instead.

Two’s Complement

Two’s complement is the standard representation for signed integers in virtually every modern architecture. It solves the double-zero problem and makes addition and subtraction work with the same hardware circuit regardless of sign.

In two’s complement with N bits:

  • The most significant bit (MSB, leftmost bit) has a negative weight of −2^(N−1), while all other bits keep their positive weights
  • All N bits still represent 2^N distinct values, split across negative and positive numbers
  • There is exactly one representation of zero

The formula for the value of a two’s complement N-bit number is:

value = −b_(N−1) × 2^(N−1)  +  Σ (b_i × 2^i)  for i from 0 to N−2

where b_i is the value of bit i.

Range of Two’s Complement

With N bits in two’s complement:

  • Minimum value: −2^(N−1) (the bit pattern 100...0, MSB = 1, all others = 0)
  • Maximum value: 2^(N−1) − 1 (the bit pattern 011...1, MSB = 0, all others = 1)
N bits Min value Max value Total range
4 −8 7 16 values
8 −128 127 256 values
16 −32 768 32 767 65 536 values
32 −2 147 483 648 2 147 483 647 ~4.3 billion values
64 −9.2 × 10^18 9.2 × 10^18 ~1.8 × 10^19 values

Notice that the total number of distinct values is always 2^N — the range is just shifted to include negative numbers.

A Concrete 4-bit Example

With 4 bits in two’s complement, the MSB has weight −2³ = −8:

Bit pattern  MSB weight  +  remaining  =  value
 0000          0             0             0
 0001          0             1             1
 0010          0             2             2
 0011          0             3             3
 0100          0             4             4
 0101          0             5             5
 0110          0             6             6
 0111          0             7             7
 1000         -8             0            -8   ← most negative
 1001         -8             1            -7
 1010         -8             2            -6
 1011         -8             3            -5
 1100         -8             4            -4
 1101         -8             5            -3
 1110         -8             6            -2
 1111         -8             7            -1

Key observations: the pattern 0000 is zero, the pattern 1000 is the most negative value (−8), and the pattern 1111 is −1 (not 15 as it would be unsigned). Positive numbers have MSB = 0; negative numbers have MSB = 1.

How to Negate a Number in Two’s Complement

To negate any N-bit two’s complement value, there is a simple two-step procedure:

  1. Flip all bits (bitwise NOT, operator ~ in Java)
  2. Add 1

Example: negate 0011 (= 3):

Step 1 — flip all bits: 0011 → 1100
Step 2 — add 1:         1100 + 0001 = 1101
Result: 1101 = −8 + 4 + 1 = −3  ✓

This procedure works in both directions: applying it to a negative number gives the corresponding positive value.

Why One More Negative Than Positive?

There is always one more representable negative value than positive value in two’s complement. This is because zero “occupies” one of the positive-side slots (the MSB = 0 half), leaving 2^(N−1) − 1 strictly positive values and 2^(N−1) negative values. The minimum value (−2^(N−1)) has no positive counterpart — attempting to negate it overflows back to itself, which is a classic source of bugs in programs that do Math.abs(Integer.MIN_VALUE) in Java.

Java’s Integer Types

Java has four signed integer primitive types, all using two’s complement:

Type Bits Min value Max value
byte 8 −128 127
short 16 −32 768 32 767
int 32 −2 147 483 648 2 147 483 647
long 64 −9 223 372 036 854 775 808 9 223 372 036 854 775 807

Java has no unsigned integer primitive. If you need unsigned 32-bit arithmetic, you either use a long and mask the upper 32 bits, or use the static helper methods in Integer added in Java 8 (Integer.toUnsignedString, Integer.compareUnsigned, etc.).

For the Secret Handshake exercise, the input is a plain int (32-bit two’s complement). Since the problem only cares about the 5 least-significant bits, the sign of the number is irrelevant after applying the mask number & 0b1_1111. That mask clears all bits above position 4, so the resulting code is always in the range [1] regardless of whether the original input was negative.

Useful Bit-Count Formulas at a Glance

Goal Formula Example (N=8)
Total distinct patterns 2^N 256
Unsigned range 0 to 2^N − 1 0 to 255
Two’s complement range −2^(N−1) to 2^(N−1) − 1 −128 to 127
Maximum positive value 2^(N−1) − 1 127
Minimum negative value −2^(N−1) −128
Value of bit at position i 2^i bit 3 = 8
Mask for the lowest N bits 2^N − 1 (or (1 << N) - 1) 0xFF for N=8

Binary Numbers and Bit Manipulation in Java

Before implementing the solution, it helps to understand how Java represents integers and how bitwise operators work.

How Integers Are Stored

In Java, an int is a 32-bit signed two’s complement integer. This means every int value occupies exactly 32 binary digits in memory. When we write the number 26, the computer stores:

00000000 00000000 00000000 00011010
                              ^^^^^
                              ||||└── bit 0 = 0 (wink off)
                              |||└──── bit 1 = 1 (double blink ON)
                              ||└────── bit 2 = 0 (close your eyes off)
                              |└─────── bit 3 = 1 (jump ON)
                              └──────── bit 4 = 1 (reverse ON)

We only care about the five least-significant bits (bits 0 through 4), and we can ignore all the others.

Java’s Binary Literal Syntax

Java allows you to write integer literals in binary using the 0b prefix:

int mask = 0b00001;  // same as writing 1
int mask = 0b10000;  // same as writing 16

The binary literal is purely a readability feature — the compiler converts it to the same integer value as the decimal equivalent. However, when working with bit masks, writing 0b00001 instead of 1 makes the intent immediately obvious to anyone reading the code.

Java also allows underscores inside numeric literals for readability:

int allFiveBits = 0b1_1111;  // same as 0b11111 = 31 = 2^5 - 1

The Bitwise AND Operator (&)

The bitwise AND operator compares two integers bit by bit. For each position, the result is 1 only if both operands have a 1 in that position; otherwise the result is 0.

  26 = 00011010
&  2 = 00000010   ← mask for "double blink" (bit 1)
─────────────────
       00000010   ← result is non-zero, so bit 1 IS set

  26 = 00011010
&  1 = 00000001   ← mask for "wink" (bit 0)
─────────────────
       00000000   ← result is zero, so bit 0 is NOT set

In Java code this looks like:

if ((number & 0b00010) != 0) {
    actions.add("double blink");
}

The expression (number & mask) != 0 is the idiomatic Java way to test whether a specific bit is set. It is a single CPU instruction and runs in O(1) time regardless of the value of number.

Other Bitwise Operators (For Reference)

While this exercise only requires &, the full set of Java bitwise operators is worth knowing:

Operator Name Behavior
& AND 1 only if both bits are 1
\| OR 1 if at least one bit is 1
^ XOR 1 if the bits differ
~ NOT flips all bits (unary)
<< Left shift shifts bits left, fills with 0 on the right
>> Signed right shift shifts bits right, fills with the sign bit on the left
>>> Unsigned right shift shifts bits right, always fills with 0 on the left

The left-shift operator is particularly useful for building masks dynamically. Instead of writing 0b00100 to check bit 2, you can write (1 << 2). More generally, (1 << i) produces a mask with exactly bit i set — a pattern you will see frequently in flag-based code.

Isolating the Relevant Bits

As a defensive measure, it is good practice to mask the input to only the five bits we care about before doing anything else:

int code = number & 0b1_1111;  // 0b11111 = 31 = 2^5 - 1, keeps only bits 0–4

This ensures that if the caller passes a number like 255 (11111111), the higher bits (111 above bit 4) do not influence the result. After this one operation, code is guaranteed to be in the range [0, 31], exactly the 32 distinct values representable in 5 unsigned bits.

Java Collections: ArrayList and Collections.reverse

The solution builds the result as a List<String> (or List<Signal> if the exercise uses an enum). Java’s List interface represents an ordered, index-accessible sequence of elements. For building a list incrementally by appending elements, the right implementation is ArrayList.

Why ArrayList?

ArrayList is backed by a dynamically resizing array. Appending an element to the end (add(element)) is amortized O(1) — meaning that while an occasional resize operation takes O(n) time to copy all elements to a larger array, the average cost per append over many operations is constant. Since we are adding at most four elements, the resize never actually happens here, and each add is a simple O(1) array write.

The alternative, LinkedList, would also work, but it uses more memory (each node carries two pointers in addition to the value) and has worse cache locality. For small, fixed-size lists like this one, ArrayList is always the better choice.

Reversing with Collections.reverse

Java’s standard library provides Collections.reverse(List<?>), which reverses a list in place — it modifies the existing list rather than creating a new one. For an ArrayList, this works by swapping elements from the two ends toward the center:

Before: [wink, double blink, jump]
Step 1: swap index 0 (wink) with index 2 (jump)   → [jump, double blink, wink]
Step 2: index 1 is the center, no swap needed
After:  [jump, double blink, wink]

This operation takes O(n) time, where n is the length of the list. Since our list has at most 4 elements, this is effectively O(1) in practice.

The Solution

With all the background in place, the implementation is remarkably concise.

SecretHandshake.java

import java.util.ArrayList;
import java.util.Collections;
import java.util.List;

class SecretHandshake {

    List<String> calculateHandshake(int number) {
        List<String> actions = new ArrayList<>();
        int code = number & 0b1_1111;  // isolate bits 0–4 (range 0 to 31)

        if ((code & 0b00001) != 0) actions.add("wink");
        if ((code & 0b00010) != 0) actions.add("double blink");
        if ((code & 0b00100) != 0) actions.add("close your eyes");
        if ((code & 0b01000) != 0) actions.add("jump");
        if ((code & 0b10000) != 0) Collections.reverse(actions);

        return actions;
    }
}

Tracing Through an Example

Let us manually trace number = 26 step by step.

number = 26

Step 1 — isolate 5 bits (2^5 - 1 = 31 = 0b11111):
  code = 26 & 0b11111
       = 0b11010 & 0b11111
       = 0b11010
       = 26  (already within [0, 31], no change)

Step 2 — check bit 0 (wink):
  code & 0b00001 = 0b11010 & 0b00001 = 0b00000 = 0  → skip

Step 3 — check bit 1 (double blink):
  code & 0b00010 = 0b11010 & 0b00010 = 0b00010 ≠ 0  → add "double blink"
  actions = ["double blink"]

Step 4 — check bit 2 (close your eyes):
  code & 0b00100 = 0b11010 & 0b00100 = 0b00000 = 0  → skip

Step 5 — check bit 3 (jump):
  code & 0b01000 = 0b11010 & 0b01000 = 0b01000 ≠ 0  → add "jump"
  actions = ["double blink", "jump"]

Step 6 — check bit 4 (reverse):
  code & 0b10000 = 0b11010 & 0b10000 = 0b10000 ≠ 0  → reverse!
  actions = ["jump", "double blink"]

Result: ["jump", "double blink"] ✓

The Variant with an Enum

If the test file imports and uses a Signal enum instead of strings, you would define a companion file:

public enum Signal {
    WINK,
    DOUBLE_BLINK,
    CLOSE_YOUR_EYES,
    JUMP
}

And update the method accordingly:

List<Signal> calculateHandshake(int number) {
    List<Signal> signals = new ArrayList<>();
    int code = number & 0b1_1111;

    if ((code & 0b00001) != 0) signals.add(Signal.WINK);
    if ((code & 0b00010) != 0) signals.add(Signal.DOUBLE_BLINK);
    if ((code & 0b00100) != 0) signals.add(Signal.CLOSE_YOUR_EYES);
    if ((code & 0b01000) != 0) signals.add(Signal.JUMP);
    if ((code & 0b10000) != 0) Collections.reverse(signals);

    return signals;
}

The logic is identical — only the element type changes.

Complexity Analysis

Understanding the complexity of a solution is not just an academic exercise. It tells you how the solution will behave under different inputs and whether it can be relied upon in contexts where performance matters.

Time Complexity

The method performs the following operations:

  1. One bitwise AND to isolate 5 bits: O(1)
  2. Four conditional bitwise AND checks: O(1) each, O(1) total (there are always exactly 4 checks, regardless of input)
  3. At most four ArrayList.add() calls: O(1) amortized each, O(1) total
  4. One optional Collections.reverse() call on a list of at most 4 elements: O(1) (constant input size)

Overall time complexity: O(1)

The entire method executes in constant time. There are no loops, no recursion, and no operations whose cost scales with the value of the input. Whether number is 1 or 2,147,483,647 (Integer.MAX_VALUE), exactly the same number of instructions are executed.

This is the best possible time complexity for a function — it cannot be improved further.

Space Complexity

The method allocates:

  • One ArrayList to hold the results: at most 4 elements, so O(1) extra space
  • One int variable code: O(1)
  • No recursive stack frames, no auxiliary data structures

Overall space complexity: O(1)

The output list itself is returned to the caller, so it is not counted as “extra” space in the standard definition of auxiliary space complexity. Even if we count the output, the list is bounded by a constant size of 4, so it remains O(1) in all cases.

Why Constant Complexity Is Possible Here

The reason both time and space complexity are O(1) is that the problem has a fixed, bounded universe. There are exactly 5 relevant bits, exactly 4 possible actions, and the reversal either happens or it does not. The problem does not scale with input size — there is no array to sort, no graph to traverse, no string to parse of variable length. The input is a single integer, and the output is a list bounded by a small constant.

This stands in contrast to a naive alternative approach that might convert the integer to its binary string representation and parse each character. That approach would still be O(1) in theory (since the string is at most 32 characters for a Java int), but it would be far slower in practice due to string allocation, Integer.toBinaryString() overhead, and character-by-character parsing. The bitwise solution avoids all of that and maps each check directly to a single CPU instruction.

Running the Tests

From IntelliJ, right-click SecretHandshakeTest.java in the Project panel and select Run ‘SecretHandshakeTest’. The test runner opens in the bottom panel and shows a green tree when all tests pass.

From the terminal, inside the secret-handshake/ directory:

./gradlew test

A successful run produces output similar to:

> Task :test

SecretHandshakeTest > wink_for_1() PASSED
SecretHandshakeTest > double_blink_for_2() PASSED
SecretHandshakeTest > close_your_eyes_for_4() PASSED
SecretHandshakeTest > jump_for_16() PASSED
SecretHandshakeTest > combine_two_actions() PASSED
SecretHandshakeTest > reverse_two_actions() PASSED
SecretHandshakeTest > reversing_one_action_gives_the_same_action() PASSED
SecretHandshakeTest > reversing_no_actions_still_gives_no_actions() PASSED
SecretHandshakeTest > all_possible_actions() PASSED
...

BUILD SUCCESSFUL in 3s
2 actionable tasks: 2 executed

Key Takeaways

Working through this exercise illustrates several principles that apply well beyond Exercism.

The most important is that choosing the right representation makes the code trivial. The number 26 looks arbitrary as a decimal. As a binary value, its meaning is self-evident once you know the encoding scheme. Recognizing when a problem maps naturally onto bit flags is a skill that takes practice, but it pays dividends in embedded systems, networking, operating systems, and performance-sensitive application code.

Understanding two’s complement and the 2^N formula is foundational. It explains why Java’s int goes up to 2 147 483 647, why there is one more negative value than positive value, and why masking with 0b1_1111 (= 2⁵ − 1 = 31) reliably isolates exactly five bits. These are not arbitrary facts — they follow directly from the mathematics of positional binary representation.

The second engineering takeaway is that the standard library is your friend. ArrayList and Collections.reverse() are not exotic choices — they are the right tools for the job, and they come with well-understood performance characteristics. Knowing when to reach for ArrayList versus LinkedList, when Collections.reverse() is in-place versus when you need a new list, and how the BOM pattern in Gradle prevents dependency version conflicts — these details compound into real engineering competence over time.

Finally, the project setup itself is instructive. A minimal Gradle project needs exactly one build.gradle, a Gradle Wrapper, and a conventional src/ directory layout. Adding complexity beyond that — extra modules, nested settings.gradle files, plugin configurations — is a choice that should be driven by a real need, not by habit or template copying.

entry.title: Software Testing in Java: Why You Should Just Write the Tests

link.title: Software Testing in Java: Why You Should Just Write the Tests

entry.content:
Let me be honest with you: for a long time, I treated tests as something you write after the code is done — a bureaucratic step you rush through before pushing to the repo. If you’ve ever thought the same, this post is for you. Because at some point it clicked: testing isn’t a chore you do after coding, it’s part of coding itself.

I think the root of the problem is how testing is often taught. It shows up at the end of a course, in a chapter that half the students skip. It’s presented as a separate discipline — something QA people do, not developers. But that framing is wrong, and it costs teams an enormous amount of time and stress.

The Real Cost of Not Testing

Think about the last time you changed a method, ran the app, manually clicked through a few screens, and convinced yourself everything was fine. We’ve all been there. It feels efficient in the moment. The problem is that manual verification doesn’t scale. As the codebase grows, the surface area of things that can silently break when you touch something grows with it — and your ability to check everything manually shrinks.

A well-placed test catches a regression in milliseconds. A missing test lets it reach production, and reach your users. Beyond that, testing gives you something less tangible but equally valuable: confidence. When your test suite is green, you can refactor aggressively, add features without anxiety, and merge pull requests without that nagging feeling that you’ve broken something somewhere. That peace of mind is not a luxury — it’s what allows a codebase to keep moving fast as it matures.

What Software Testing Actually Is

At its core, software testing is the process of evaluating and verifying that a software product functions correctly, securely, and as intended. It splits into two broad families. The first is dynamic testing — actually running the software and checking its outputs against expected results. The second is static testing — reviewing code, documentation, or design artifacts without executing them. Think code reviews, linting, and static analysis tools like SpotBugs or SonarQube.

Both approaches are useful and complementary. But as developers writing application code day to day, dynamic testing — and unit testing in particular — is where most of our leverage is. It’s fast, it’s local, and it runs on every build.

The Four Levels of Testing

Testing doesn’t happen at a single level. It unfolds across a spectrum of abstraction, each level targeting a different scope of the system.

Unit testing is the most granular. It tests individual methods and classes in complete isolation from the rest of the system. This is the developer’s primary responsibility. Integration testing comes next: it verifies that separate components work correctly when combined — that your service talks to your repository as expected, that your API layer correctly calls your business logic. System testing then validates the entire application against its functional requirements, typically owned by a QA team. Finally, acceptance testing answers the highest-level question of all: does the software actually meet the real needs of its users and stakeholders?

Level What It Tests Who Typically Runs It
Unit Testing Individual methods and classes in isolation Developers
Integration Testing Interaction between combined components Developers / QA
System Testing The entire application against requirements QA team
Acceptance Testing Whether the software meets real user/business needs Stakeholders / Clients

As developers, we own the bottom two levels. Understanding the upper levels helps us write better unit and integration tests that don’t leave dangerous blind spots.

Other Testing Types Worth Knowing

Beyond those four levels, a few specialized categories come up regularly in real projects and are worth having in your vocabulary.

Regression testing confirms that new changes haven’t broken existing functionality. It’s the bedrock of CI/CD pipelines — the suite that runs automatically on every push. Smoke testing is a quick sanity check that the most critical paths still work after a new build, before investing time in deeper testing. Performance testing evaluates how the system behaves under load — response times, throughput, and stability under stress. Security testing proactively identifies vulnerabilities before attackers find them. And exploratory testing is the unscripted, curiosity-driven kind, where a tester actively looks for unexpected behaviour with no predefined script to follow.

You won’t always need all of these, but knowing they exist means you’ll recognize when to reach for them.

JUnit 5 in Practice

Now let’s get concrete. JUnit 5 — also known as JUnit Jupiter — is the standard unit testing framework for Java. It’s mature, expressive, and integrates natively with Maven, Gradle, IntelliJ IDEA, and Eclipse. If you write Java professionally, you will use it.

Setting Up

For Maven, add this to your pom.xml:

<dependency>
    <groupId>org.junit.jupiter</groupId>
    <artifactId>junit-jupiter</artifactId>
    <version>5.10.2</version>
    <scope>test</scope>
</dependency>

For Gradle:

testImplementation 'org.junit.jupiter:junit-jupiter:5.10.2'

The Test Lifecycle

One of the things I appreciate most about JUnit 5 is how explicitly it models the lifecycle of a test. Before any test runs, you can set up state. After each test, you can clean it up. The annotations that control this are:

Annotation When It Runs
@BeforeAll Once before all tests in the class
@BeforeEach Before every single test method
@Test The test itself
@AfterEach After every single test method
@AfterAll Once after all tests in the class

The golden rule is: never share mutable state between tests. Each test should start with a clean slate. @BeforeEach is the tool for that:

class OrderServiceTest {

    private OrderService orderService;

    @BeforeEach
    void setUp() {
        orderService = new OrderService(); // fresh instance for every test
    }

    @AfterEach
    void tearDown() {
        // cleanup if needed (e.g. close resources)
    }
}

Basic Tests and Assertions

Let’s start with something simple — a Calculator class:

// Calculator.java
public class Calculator {
    public int add(int a, int b)        { return a + b; }
    public int subtract(int a, int b)   { return a - b; }
    public int multiply(int a, int b)   { return a * b; }
    public int divide(int a, int b)     { return a / b; }
}

// CalculatorTest.java
import org.junit.jupiter.api.*;
import static org.junit.jupiter.api.Assertions.*;

class CalculatorTest {

    private Calculator calculator;

    @BeforeEach
    void setUp() {
        calculator = new Calculator();
    }

    @Test
    @DisplayName("4 + 6 should equal 10")
    void testAdd() {
        assertEquals(10, calculator.add(4, 6));
    }

    @Test
    @DisplayName("Dividing by zero should throw ArithmeticException")
    void testDivideByZero() {
        assertThrows(ArithmeticException.class, () -> calculator.divide(10, 0));
    }

    @Test
    @DisplayName("Multiply result should be positive and correct")
    void testMultiplyAssertAll() {
        int result = calculator.multiply(3, 4);
        assertAll("multiply checks",
            () -> assertNotNull(result),
            () -> assertTrue(result > 0),
            () -> assertEquals(12, result)
        );
    }
}

Notice assertAll() in that last test. Unlike stacking multiple assertEquals calls, assertAll() runs every assertion inside it and reports all failures at once, rather than stopping at the first. When debugging a failing test, that difference is huge.

Parameterized Tests

This is where JUnit 5 really earns its keep. Rather than duplicating a test method for every input combination you want to cover, @ParameterizedTest lets you express the same logic once and feed it a table of data:

import org.junit.jupiter.params.ParameterizedTest;
import org.junit.jupiter.params.provider.CsvSource;
import org.junit.jupiter.params.provider.ValueSource;
import static org.junit.jupiter.api.Assertions.*;

class CalculatorParameterizedTest {

    private final Calculator calculator = new Calculator();

    @ParameterizedTest
    @ValueSource(ints = {1, 2, 3, 100, -5})
    @DisplayName("Adding zero should always return the same number")
    void testAddZero(int number) {
        assertEquals(number, calculator.add(number, 0));
    }

    @ParameterizedTest(name = "{0} + {1} = {2}")
    @CsvSource({
        "1,  2,  3",
        "5,  5, 10",
        "-3, 3,  0",
        "0,  0,  0"
    })
    void testAddWithMultipleInputs(int a, int b, int expected) {
        assertEquals(expected, calculator.add(a, b));
    }
}

@ValueSource handles single-argument tests cleanly. @CsvSource is perfect for multi-column tabular data, and the name attribute even formats the test name in the output, making failures immediately readable. For more complex objects, @MethodSource lets you supply a Stream<Arguments> from a static factory method.

Nested Tests

@Nested classes let you group related tests under a shared context, giving your test file a logical hierarchy that mirrors your domain:

@DisplayName("Calculator Tests")
class CalculatorNestedTest {

    private Calculator calculator = new Calculator();

    @Nested
    @DisplayName("Addition")
    class AdditionTests {
        @Test void addsPositiveNumbers()  { assertEquals(5,  calculator.add(2, 3));   }
        @Test void addsNegativeNumbers()  { assertEquals(-5, calculator.add(-2, -3)); }
        @Test void addsMixedNumbers()     { assertEquals(1,  calculator.add(4, -3));  }
    }

    @Nested
    @DisplayName("Division")
    class DivisionTests {
        @Test void dividesTwoNumbers()    { assertEquals(2, calculator.divide(10, 5)); }
        @Test void throwsOnDivideByZero() {
            assertThrows(ArithmeticException.class, () -> calculator.divide(5, 0));
        }
    }
}

When these run in your IDE, the test results tree mirrors the nested structure exactly. It reads almost like a specification document, which is precisely the point.

Mocking with Mockito

Real-world classes rarely live in isolation. A UserService depends on a UserRepository. A PaymentService calls an external gateway. You don’t want your unit test to spin up a real database or make real HTTP calls — so you mock the dependency, replacing it with a controlled fake that you can instruct to return specific values.

Mockito is the standard library for this in Java. Add it alongside JUnit 5:

<dependency>
    <groupId>org.mockito</groupId>
    <artifactId>mockito-junit-jupiter</artifactId>
    <version>5.12.0</version>
    <scope>test</scope>
</dependency>

Then wire it in with @ExtendWith:

import org.junit.jupiter.api.Test;
import org.junit.jupiter.api.extension.ExtendWith;
import org.mockito.InjectMocks;
import org.mockito.Mock;
import org.mockito.junit.jupiter.MockitoExtension;
import java.util.Optional;
import static org.mockito.Mockito.*;
import static org.junit.jupiter.api.Assertions.*;

@ExtendWith(MockitoExtension.class)
class UserServiceTest {

    @Mock
    private UserRepository userRepository;  // fake, fully controlled by us

    @InjectMocks
    private UserService userService;        // the class under test

    @Test
    @DisplayName("Should return user when found by ID")
    void testGetUserById() {
        User user = new User(1, "Mario");
        when(userRepository.findById(1)).thenReturn(Optional.of(user));

        User result = userService.getUserById(1);

        assertEquals("Mario", result.getName());
        verify(userRepository, times(1)).findById(1);
    }

    @Test
    @DisplayName("Should throw exception when user not found")
    void testGetUserByIdNotFound() {
        when(userRepository.findById(99)).thenReturn(Optional.empty());
        assertThrows(UserNotFoundException.class, () -> userService.getUserById(99));
    }
}

@Mock creates a fake UserRepository. @InjectMocks automatically wires it into UserService. when(...).thenReturn(...) defines the fake’s behaviour for a specific input. And verify(...) asserts that the mock was actually called the expected number of times — so you’re not just checking the return value, you’re checking the interaction itself.

The TDD Mindset

All of the above becomes even more powerful when you flip the order: write the test before the code. This is Test-Driven Development (TDD), and it follows a short loop:

  1. Red — write a test for behaviour that doesn’t exist yet; watch it fail
  2. Green — write the minimum code to make it pass
  3. Refactor — clean up the code freely, knowing the test has your back

Writing the test first forces you to think about the interface and behaviour of your code before you think about the implementation. You end up with smaller, more focused methods, clearer responsibilities, and a test suite that grows naturally alongside your production code rather than being retrofitted after the fact.

Running Your Tests

  • IntelliJ IDEA / Eclipse: right-click the test class or method → Run
  • Maven: mvn test
  • Gradle: gradle test

Your build tool will generate a report under target/surefire-reports (Maven) or build/reports/tests (Gradle) with a full breakdown of passed, failed, and skipped tests.

Writing tests is one of those habits that feels slightly slower at first and then, quietly, makes everything faster. The codebase stays cleaner, refactoring becomes less scary, and bugs get caught before users ever see them. Your future self — staring at a green CI pipeline at 11pm before a release — will be grateful.
entry.summary: A personal take on why testing should be a natural habit when writing code, and a detailed guide on how to do it in Java with JUnit 5.

entry.title: My Coding Best Practices
entry.content:
Every developer, at some point, opens a file they wrote six months ago and wonders what they were thinking. The code works — technically — but it’s hard to read, harder to change, and terrifying to touch. I’ve been there too.

Over time, I built a set of practices that I apply every time I sit down to write code. They’re not rules I follow blindly — they’re habits I developed by making mistakes, reading other people’s code, and slowly learning what makes a codebase a pleasure to work in rather than a burden. This post is my attempt to write them all down in one place.

None of these are language-specific. Whether you write Java, Python, or JavaScript, the underlying principles are the same.

1. Use a Proper IDE

Before writing a single line of code, set yourself up with the right environment. An IDE (Integrated Development Environment) is not just a text editor — it’s a tool that understands your code. It autocompletes method names and imports as you type, highlights errors before you even run the program, lets you rename a variable across the entire codebase in one operation, and integrates with Git so you never have to leave the editor to commit or review changes.

That removed friction adds up. The less time you spend fighting your tools, the more mental space you have for logic and design — which is where the real work happens.

Here are the tools worth knowing:

Language IDE Notes
Any VS Code Free, open source, highly extensible via plugins
Java IntelliJ IDEA Community Free, best-in-class Java support
Python PyCharm Community Free, excellent Python tooling
Any Eclipse Free, open source, mature ecosystem
Any Neovim Free, keyboard-driven, highly configurable

If you use VS Code, three extensions are worth installing from day one:

  • GitLens — rich Git history and inline blame annotations
  • SonarLint — real-time code quality and security analysis
  • Error Lens — displays errors and warnings inline, right next to the code

2. Write Code for Humans First

The machine doesn’t care what you name your variables. Your colleagues — and your future self — very much do. Code is read far more often than it is written, so always optimize for the reader.

// Hard to read — what does this do?
public double calc(double a, int b, double c) {
    return a * b * (1 - c);
}

// Clear — reads almost like a sentence
public double calculateFinalPrice(double unitPrice, int quantity, double discountRate) {
    return unitPrice * quantity * (1 - discountRate);
}

The second version needs no comment to be understood. That clarity is a choice, and it’s one worth making every time.

A few rules of thumb to keep in mind:

  • Variable names should explain what they store, not how (userList, not data)
  • Method names should describe what they do (sendWelcomeEmail(), not process())
  • Keep methods short — if a method doesn’t fit on one screen, it probably does too much

Tools like SonarQube Community Edition, PMD, and Checkstyle can help enforce these standards automatically across a Java project.

3. The SOLID Principles

As a codebase grows, it tends to rot in predictable ways: classes that accumulate responsibilities over time, code that breaks when you try to extend it, dependencies that are impossible to swap out for testing. SOLID is a set of five design principles that address exactly these failure modes.

Principle What It Means Practical Example
Single Responsibility A class should do one thing only UserValidator validates; it does not save to the database
Open/Closed Open for extension, closed for modification Add new behaviour via new classes, not by editing existing ones
Liskov Substitution Subclasses must be usable wherever their parent is used A Square subclass should not break code written for a Rectangle
Interface Segregation Prefer many small, focused interfaces over one large one Printable and Serializable as separate interfaces, not one Utility
Dependency Inversion Depend on abstractions, not concrete implementations Inject a DatabaseInterface, not a specific MySQLDatabase

Each of these principles deserves more space than a table can give them. I’ll go deeper into each one with practical Java examples in a dedicated follow-up post.

4. Don’t Repeat Yourself (DRY)

If the same logic appears in two places, it will eventually be updated in one and forgotten in the other. This is one of the most common sources of subtle, hard-to-trace bugs.

// Bad — the same logic duplicated in two different places
String email = input.trim().toLowerCase(); // in the registration flow
String email = input.trim().toLowerCase(); // in the password reset flow

// Good — extracted once, reused everywhere
private String normalizeEmail(String input) {
    return input.trim().toLowerCase();
}

Every piece of logic should have a single, authoritative home in the codebase. When it needs to change — and it will — you change it in exactly one place and can be confident the fix propagates everywhere it needs to.

5. Comment Why, Not What

The code already shows what it does. A good comment explains why a non-obvious decision was made. Commenting obvious things creates noise that drowns out the comments that actually matter.

// Bad — the code already says this
i = i + 1; // increment i

// Good — explains a non-obvious constraint
i += 1; // offset by 1 because the external API uses 1-based indexing

Three rules to follow:

  • Comment on business rules, edge cases, and non-obvious algorithmic choices
  • Never comment out dead code — delete it. Git keeps the history
  • Always update a comment when you update the code it describes. A wrong comment is worse than no comment

6. Handle Errors Explicitly

Silent failures are a debugging nightmare. When something goes wrong and nothing is logged, you have no idea where to start looking.

// Bad — the error is swallowed silently
try {
    result = fetchUserData(userId);
} catch (Exception e) {
    // nothing
}

// Good — caught specifically, logged with context, re-thrown meaningfully
try {
    result = fetchUserData(userId);
} catch (NetworkException e) {
    logger.error("Failed to fetch user {}: {}", userId, e.getMessage(), e);
    throw new ServiceUnavailableException("User data temporarily unavailable", e);
}

Key habits:

  • Always catch the most specific exception type you can — a bare catch (Exception e) hides bugs
  • Log errors with enough context to reconstruct what happened: include IDs, inputs, and the original exception
  • Never expose raw stack traces to end users
  • Define custom exception classes to distinguish different failure modes from each other

7. Use Git — and Use It Well

Git is not just a backup tool. It is a communication tool. Your commit history tells the story of your project and lets anyone — including future you — understand why a decision was made months after the fact.

# Bad — tells you nothing
git commit -m "fix stuff"

# Good — tells you exactly what changed and why
git commit -m "fix: handle null user in authentication flow"

Conventional Commits is a lightweight standard worth adopting. The prefixes you’ll use most often are feat: for new features, fix: for bug fixes, refactor: for code restructuring without behaviour change, docs: for documentation updates, and test: for anything test-related.

Pull Requests

A Pull Request (PR) is a formal proposal to merge a branch of code into another — usually main. When you open one, you give teammates the chance to review your changes line by line, ask questions, and run automated checks via CI/CD before anything reaches the main branch. Even on solo projects, opening a PR and reviewing your own diff before merging catches a surprising number of obvious mistakes.

Keep PRs small and focused — 200 to 400 lines is a good target. Large PRs don’t get reviewed carefully; they get rubber-stamped. And three non-negotiable rules: never commit directly to main, never commit secrets or passwords, and always add sensitive files to .gitignore.

Two tools worth adding to your workflow:

  • pre-commit — run linting, formatting, and secret scanning automatically before every commit
  • act — run your GitHub Actions pipeline locally before pushing

8. Test Your Code

Untested code is code you cannot safely change. Tests are what give you the confidence to refactor, upgrade dependencies, and ship features without fear.

There are three levels of testing:

  • Unit tests — test individual methods in isolation. Fast and precise. This is a developer’s primary responsibility
  • Integration tests — verify that separate components work correctly together (a service correctly calling a repository, for example)
  • End-to-end tests — validate the full user flow from input to output

A quick example in Java with JUnit:

@Test
public void testCalculateFinalPrice_basicCase() {
    // $10 item, 3 units, 10% discount → $27.00
    assertEquals(27.00, calculator.calculateFinalPrice(10.0, 3, 0.10), 0.001);
}

@Test
public void testCalculateFinalPrice_noDiscount() {
    assertEquals(30.00, calculator.calculateFinalPrice(10.0, 3, 0.0), 0.001);
}

@Test
public void testCalculateFinalPrice_fullDiscount() {
    assertEquals(0.0, calculator.calculateFinalPrice(10.0, 3, 1.0), 0.001);
}

If you’re afraid to refactor something, that’s a signal you need more tests. Tests should be fast, isolated, and deterministic — no random data, no network calls, no shared state between test cases.

Language Testing Framework Mocking Library
Java JUnit 5 Mockito
JavaScript Jest Built-in
Python pytest unittest.mock

9. Automate Formatting and Linting

Inconsistent formatting is cognitive noise. When a codebase mixes tabs and spaces, or uses different brace styles across different files, every code review becomes a style debate instead of a logic discussion. The solution: automate it and never discuss it again.

The two tools you need are a formatter and a linter, and they do different things.

A formatter is purely cosmetic. It rewrites your code to conform to a consistent visual style — indentation, spacing, line breaks, brace placement. It doesn’t care about what your code does, only how it looks. You run it, and the file comes out formatted the same way every time, regardless of who wrote it.

A linter goes deeper. It analyzes your source code without executing it, looking for things that are technically valid but likely wrong: an unused variable, a function that’s grown too complex, a pattern known to cause bugs, a potential null pointer, a security vulnerability. It works by parsing your code into a structured representation and checking it against a set of rules — then reporting exactly which line violates which rule and why. Think of it as a second pair of eyes that never gets tired and never misses the same mistake twice.

Together, a formatter handles style and a linter handles quality. Both run automatically, no human judgement required.

Language Formatter Linter
Java google-java-format Checkstyle
JavaScript Prettier ESLint
Python Black Ruff

Add both to your CI/CD pipeline so they run automatically on every PR. If they’re not automated, they won’t be consistent.

10. Refactor Continuously

“Always leave the code cleaner than you found it.”

Good code is not written once and left alone — it is refined over time. Small, continuous refactors prevent technical debt from accumulating into an unmaintainable mess.

The signals are usually obvious: a method with more than three or four parameters, the same logic in multiple places, a class that has grown past two or three hundred lines, or that vague anxiety you feel before touching a particular file. When you notice any of these, take a few minutes to clean it up before moving on.

You don’t need a dedicated refactoring sprint. A few minutes of cleanup every time you touch a file is enough to keep a codebase healthy over the long term.

11. Don’t Optimize Prematurely

“Premature optimization is the root of all evil.” — Donald Knuth

The correct priority order is always: make it work → make it clear → make it fast. Optimizing before you have a measured performance problem leads to complex, hard-to-read code that solves a problem you don’t actually have.

Write the clearest solution first. Then, if performance becomes an issue, use a profiler to find where the real bottleneck is, and optimize only that specific part.

Don't guess. Measure.

Profiling tools worth knowing: VisualVM and async-profiler for Java, Chrome DevTools Performance panel for JavaScript, and py-spy for Python.

12. Separate Your Concerns

Keep different responsibilities in different parts of your code. The classic pattern is a three-layer architecture:

Presentation layer   →  handles input and output (UI, API endpoints)
Business logic layer →  contains the rules of your application
Data layer           →  handles storage and retrieval

When these layers bleed into each other — database queries inside UI components, business rules scattered across API handlers — you end up with classes that are impossible to test, reuse, or safely change. The boundary between layers doesn’t need to be rigid, but it does need to exist and be respected.

13. Never Hardcode Configuration

Hardcoding URLs, credentials, feature flags, or environment-specific values in source code is both a security risk and a maintenance problem.

// Bad — credentials in source code
Connection db = DriverManager.getConnection(
    "jdbc:postgresql://prod-server/mydb", "admin", "secret123"
);

// Good — read from the environment at runtime
String dbUrl = System.getenv("DATABASE_URL");
Connection db = DriverManager.getConnection(dbUrl);

Store secrets in .env files locally — always listed in .gitignore. In production, use environment variables or a dedicated secret manager. Useful libraries for loading .env files: dotenv-java for Java, dotenv for JavaScript, and python-dotenv for Python. For production secrets at scale, HashiCorp Vault is the open source standard.

14. Take Code Review Seriously

Code reviews exist not just to catch bugs, but to share knowledge and raise the quality standard of the whole team. How you participate on both sides matters.

As an author: keep PRs small and focused, explain non-obvious choices in the PR description, and review your own diff before requesting a review — you’ll catch most obvious mistakes yourself.

As a reviewer: ask questions instead of issuing directives. “Could this be null here?” lands better than “This will crash.” Approve good-enough code — perfect is the enemy of shipped — and make a point of noting good patterns, not only criticising bad ones.

15. How to Approach a Problem Before Writing Code

One of the most common mistakes developers make — especially early on — is opening the editor before they fully understand the problem. The result is code that solves the wrong thing, or solves the right thing in the wrong way, and has to be thrown away.

Here is the process I follow every time I need to solve something and translate it into code:

  1. Understand the problem fully before touching the keyboard. Read the requirements carefully. What is the input? What is the expected output? What are the edge cases — empty input, null values, very large data, invalid formats? Write these down. You cannot write a correct solution to a problem you haven’t fully understood.

  2. Break it down into smaller sub-problems. Almost every problem is a composition of simpler ones. Decompose it until each piece is small enough that you can describe it in one sentence. A function that does one clear, describable thing is a function you can write, test, and reason about.

  3. Think about the solution in plain language first. Before writing a single line of code, describe your approach in plain English — or pseudocode if you prefer. What data structures will you use? What is the order of operations? Where could things go wrong? If you can’t explain it clearly in words, you don’t understand it well enough to code it yet.

  4. Write the test before the implementation. Define what “correct” looks like before you try to be correct. Writing the test first forces you to think about the interface and behaviour of your code from the outside — which is exactly how users and other parts of the system will interact with it.

  5. Write the simplest solution that works. Resist the urge to be clever. The goal of the first version is correctness, not elegance. Get it working, verify it against your tests and edge cases, then look at whether it needs to be made clearer or faster.

  6. Refactor once it’s working. With a passing test suite as your safety net, you can now clean up freely. Extract repeated logic, rename things for clarity, simplify control flow. This is the step where good code is actually made.

The discipline here is resisting the pull to jump straight to step five. Spending five minutes thinking clearly at the start saves hours of confused debugging later.

Concepts Worth Understanding Deeply

Beyond day-to-day practices, these are the foundational ideas that will genuinely level up how you think about software. You don’t need to master all of them at once, but each one is worth spending time with:

  • Big O notation — reason about algorithm performance before profiling
  • Design patterns — Factory, Singleton, Observer, Strategy, Decorator. Shared vocabulary for common solutions
  • CAP theorem — fundamental trade-offs in distributed systems
  • ACID vs BASE — the two competing models for database transaction reliability
  • REST vs GraphQL — trade-offs between the two dominant API design philosophies
  • Immutability and pure functions — the foundation of functional programming and a powerful tool for eliminating side-effect bugs
  • Concurrency and race conditions — essential for writing correct multi-threaded or async code
  • The Twelve-Factor App — a methodology for building scalable, portable software (12factor.net)

These are not rules to follow blindly. They are principles developed by generations of developers through experience — and, more importantly, through mistakes. Start with the ones most relevant to your current project, apply them consistently, and build the habit from there.

The goal is not a perfect codebase. It’s a codebase that you and your team can read, understand, and confidently change six months from now. That’s the whole game.
